plateReadeR reads output files from plate readers into a tidy table and offers a few basic quality control (QC) steps. This vignette walks through the whole workflow on a LogPhase600 plate: read, flag, blank-correct, smooth and plot. Joining the data to sample metadata is left to you.

```{r setup}
library(plateReadeR)
```

## Read

Each reader returns one row per well per time point. Time is in elapsed seconds/hours. These are snapped to a regular grid with `snap_hours()`, so that plates from different runs are harmonized and can later be joined or aligned. This is necessary because there is sometimes some drift that prevents joining by elapsed time.

| Function | Instrument | Format |
|---|---|---|
| `read_logphase_txt()` | LogPhase600 | text, one file per plate |
| `read_logphase_xlsx()` | LogPhase600 | Excel; `sheet = "raw"`, `"results"` or `"procedure"`, all plates combined. Returns one tibble for all plates |
| `read_synergy_xlsx()` | Synergy H1 | Excel time course; `sheet = "raw"`, `"results"` or `"setup"` |
| `read_synergy_endpoint()` | Synergy H1 | Excel single time point |
| `read_bioscreen()` | Bioscreen C | UTF-16 text or csv, one or two 100-well plates |

```{r read}
f <- system.file("extdata", "logphase600_plate1.txt", package = "plateReadeR")
d <- read_logphase_txt(f)
d
```

Excel exports hold several different sheets for each plate. The most useful one is the "Raw Data" sheet but sometimes the "Summary" sheet is useful to determine how the Logphase600 calculated different growth parameters (e.g., lagtime and growth rate). The "Procedure" sheet describes the different technical specifications of the run. The funcitons `read_logphase_xlsx()` and `read_synergy_xlsx()` can read each of these sheet types using the paramter `sheet`. The procedure sheet is parsed into one row per plate:

```{r sheets}
xf <- system.file(
  "extdata",
  "logphase600_example.xlsx",
  package = "plateReadeR"
)
read_logphase_xlsx(xf, sheet = "procedure")[c(
  "plate_id",
  "runtime_hours",
  "interval_hours",
  "shaking_rpm",
  "wavelength_nm",
  "temperature_setpoint_c"
)]
```

Wells are only identified using `plate_id` and `well`, in every reader. You will need to join these to your own metadata file to make them unique across runs.

## Flag saturated and negative OD

`flag_od_range()` adds well-level flags for wells that have either negative OD values or values that exceed a threshold value. This `saturation` value needs to be selected by the user. There is no default.

```{r flag-range}
d <- flag_od_range(d, saturation = 2)
table(unique(d[c("well", "flag_saturated", "flag_negative")])[-1])
```

## Blank-correct

If you plate has blank wells (it should!) `blank_correct()` can subtract blank wells from all other wells, with an OD floor at 0. With no `blank` supplied, it is assumed that the first 5 reads in a well are not measuring growth so these are averaged as a "pseudo-blank" and then subtracted.

```{r blank}
d <- blank_correct(d)
d[d$well == "A09", c("hours", "od", "blank_od", "od_corrected")][1:5, ]
```

Alternatively, you can name the blank wells. They are matched by time  within the same plate. If multiple blanks are supplied they are averaged. (Not run here, because which wells are blanks depends on your plate layout.)

```{r blank-wells, eval = FALSE}
blanks <- data.frame(plate_id = "Plate 1", well = c("A01", "B01"))
blank_correct(d, blank = blanks)
```

## Flag wells with no growth

`flag_no_growth()` flags wells whose corrected OD never increases past the `min_rise` OD threshold. The default of 0.05 is a starting point: check it against wells you know do and do not grow.

```{r no-growth}
d <- flag_no_growth(d, min_rise = 0.05)
table(unique(d[c("well", "flag_no_growth")])$flag_no_growth)
```

## Smooth

Smoothing is off by default. `smooth_od()` applies a 5-point centered rolling mean to each well. It adds `od_corrected_rollmean`, leaving the raw and corrected columns intact. (`blank_correct(smooth = TRUE)` does the same in one step.)

```{r smooth}
d <- smooth_od(d)
names(d)
```

## Plot

`plot_plate()` draws one panel per well for one plate. Curve color shows QC status. A well with no flags is `"ok"`, and a well with several flags shows them joined with `+`. With `smooth = TRUE` the smoothed curve is overlaid on the raw one.

```{r plot, fig.height = 7}
plot_plate(d, plate = "Plate 1", smooth = TRUE)
```


## A Bioscreen run

`read_bioscreen()` handles the Bioscreen C text export, which is UTF-16 with comma decimals; both are detected and converted automatically. A Bioscreen C run holds one or two 100-well plates, with wells 1 to 100 on plate 1 and 101 to 200 on plate 2. Wells are named by a zero-padded `well` within each `plate_id` (`"001"` to `"100"`), so the key is the same `plate_id` and `well` pair as for the LogPhase600. The position in the run (1 to 200) is kept as `well_index`. The `Blank` column the instrument writes is always zero (don't understand what this is for). This is dropped by default.

The file below is a complete two-plate run, 567 reads at about 5-minute intervals over 47 hours, stored xz-compressed (readers can read compressed files directly).

```{r bioscreen-read}
bf <- system.file("extdata", "bioscreen_full.txt.xz", package = "plateReadeR")
b <- read_bioscreen(bf)
b
```

The same QC steps from the logphase600 apply to the bioscreen. Here the smoothed curve is added during blank correction with `smooth = TRUE`.

```{r bioscreen-qc}
b <- b |>
  flag_od_range(saturation = 2) |>
  blank_correct(smooth = TRUE) |>
  flag_no_growth()

unique(b[c(
  "plate_id",
  "well",
  "flag_saturated",
  "flag_negative",
  "flag_no_growth"
)]) |>
  subset(select = -well) |>
  aggregate(
    cbind(flag_saturated, flag_negative, flag_no_growth) ~ plate_id,
    data = _,
    FUN = sum
  )
```

Wells on a Bioscreen plate are laid out as a square grid of numbers rather than lettered rows, so `plot_plate()` draws them as a 10 by 10 grid.

```{r bioscreen-plot, fig.height = 9}
plot_plate(b, plate = "Plate 2", smooth = TRUE)
```
